newsitem.title: USA: IMF backs limited SDR issue, but at odds over size.
newsitem.headline: IMF backs limited SDR issue, but at odds over size.

text.p: The IMF has given the thumbs-up to a plan that would pump billions of dollars into the world economy through a limited issue of its artificial currency, international monetary sources said Monday.
But the sources, who declined to be named, said the International Monetary Fund board remains divided over the size of the allocation of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs).
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus proposed a 26 billion SDR issue, worth about $37-1/2 billion at current exchange rates. But a number of industrial nations opposed that as too large.

Under the plan, each of the IMF's 181 member nations would receive some SDRs. But the bulk of the money would go to the more than 35 nations that have joined the Fund since the last SDR issue in 1981 in a so-called "equity" allocation.
In issuing SDRs, the IMF basically creates money out of thin air, beefing up member nations' currency reserves and effectively giving them extra borrowing power.
At the IMF's annual meeting two years ago in Madrid, Spain, rich and poor nations deadlocked over the SDR issue in an unusual public battle.
At that time, Camdessus -- backed by developing nations -- was pushing for a broad-based 36-billion SDR allocation to meet what he said was a global need for liquidity.
But industrial countries refused to go along and instead only offered a limited "equity" issue worth 16 billion SDR, or about $23 billion.
The board's decision to back an equity allocation now, rather than a broad-based SDR issue, means that the industrial countries have basically won the argument.

International monetary sources said they expect the eventual equity allocation to total somewhere between 16 billion to 26 billion SDR. One source said it will probably end up "substantially" more than 16 billion SDR.
